newsitem.title: USA: NASA chief says space program better under Clinton.
newsitem.headline: NASA chief says space program better under Clinton.

text.p: President Bill Clinton had been better for the U.S. space programme than predecessor George Bush, NASA adminstrator Daniel Goldin said on Friday in a casual conversation captured on NASA television.
Goldin, a former aerospace executive whom Bush appointed to his current post in March 1992, said Bush talked a better game than he played for the space programme.

"I told (Clinton) I joined the space programme because of John Kennedy and I'm staying because of him," Goldin told Johnson Space Centre director George Abbey during a pause in a ceremony welcoming home astronauts from a space shuttle mission completed on Thursday.
"Despite all the hits, I think he's done a better job for NASA than Bush. Bush said the right things, but never executed," Goldin said. Abbey's reply was inaudible.
NASA's budget has been cut by 30 percent during the past two years, but funding for a controversial $30 billion space station has remained largely intact during the Clinton administration.

Goldin also told Abbey "I liked what I said about him," referring to his introduction for Clinton at the ceremony to congratulate astronaut Shannon Lucid on her return from a record-breaking six-month stay on Russian space station Mir.
In the introduction, Goldin praised Clinton for "fighting every day for the space programme through countless votes, over and over again, but winning every one of them."
Clinton, on a campaign swing through Texas, praised Lucid's stay on Mir -- the longest by a U.S. astronaut -- as an "amazing, amazing achievement."

Lucid was ferried home by the shuttle Atlantis crew. After landing on Thursday at Kennedy Space Centre in Florida, the astronauts flew on Friday to Houston, where they were met at Ellington Field by Clinton and several hundred well-wishers.

Clinton, finished with his brief speech, had left the ceremony and was walking to his helicopter when Goldin and Abbey, awaiting his take-off, held their conversation near a microphone on the speakers' podium.
NASA Select, the agency's broadcast channel, was televising the event.
